reason: The intro says to follow the stem-cell branch into neural progenitors, and the induction environment shows signals acting on those cells.
expectation: A subset of the stem cells should become neural progenitors.

effect: The signals produced neural progenitors, which can lead to neurons and supporting cells.
reaction: The branching paths make me curious how the different cells will develop.
reason: The neuronal differentiation signals are pictured acting on neural progenitors, matching the goal of building neurons.
expectation: The progenitors should develop toward neurons, with the beginnings of their cell processes.

effect: The progenitors became neuron cell bodies with buds where dendrites and axons can extend.
reaction: The buds make the next construction step clear.
reason: The dendrites have bases that match the cell-body stubs and will add the receiving branches named in the goal.
expectation: The neuron cell bodies should gain branching dendrites for receiving signals.

effect: The cell bodies now have receiving branches; they still need axons to meet the goal.
reaction: The picture makes it clear the branches are parts of the same cells.
reason: The axons have ends matching the cell bodies and provide the conducting processes named in the goal.
expectation: The neurons should gain long axons and terminals for carrying signals.

effect: The neurons now have both dendrites and axons, and the next goal is to connect and support them.
reaction: The travelling membrane change is a useful distinction from something moving inside the axon.
reason: The excitatory contacts show how an axon terminal communicates with a receiving cell, so they fit the goal of connecting neurons.
expectation: The neurons should gain connections that can pass excitatory signals between them.

effect: The neurons now have excitatory connections, including two inputs converging on one receiving neuron.
reaction: The small gaps make it clearer that the connected neurons remain separate cells.
reason: The inhibitory contacts show how another input can affect whether a receiving neuron reaches the firing threshold.
expectation: The network should gain inhibitory connections alongside its excitatory ones.

effect: The circuit now shows how excitatory and inhibitory inputs combine to affect whether a neuron fires. It still needs supporting cells and a change at a synapse.
reaction: The two voltage traces make inhibition's effect clearer.
reason: Astrocytes are supporting cells shown taking up potassium and released transmitter near synapses, so they fit the goal of supporting the circuit.
expectation: The circuit should gain astrocyte support around its connections.

alternatives.reason: Their myelin sleeves could also support the neurons' axons.

effect: Astrocytes are now interwoven with the circuit; the axon sleeves and synapse change remain to explore.
reaction: The supporting cells fit around the existing neurons without replacing them.
reason: The oligodendrocytes have myelin sleeves that fit along axons, so they are a clear next step in supporting the neurons.
expectation: The circuit should gain myelin sleeves around its axons.

effect: The circuit now includes both supporting cell types, with myelin on selected axon stretches. The remaining goal is to examine a synapse changing.
reaction: The picture distinguishes the receiving cell's receptor vesicles from the sending cell's transmitter vesicles.
reason: Repeated paired activity is shown at an existing connection, matching the goal of examining a change at one synapse.
expectation: Repeated activity should strengthen the highlighted connection between neurons.

effect: The final result shows that repeated paired activity strengthened one connection's local response without making travelling impulses larger. Both chapter goals are complete.
reaction: The before-and-after comparison was surprising because the change stayed at one connection.

mostWorthwhile.text: Adding inhibitory contacts was most worthwhile: the paired voltage traces showed how inhibition can keep a neuron from firing even when it receives excitation.

leastWorthwhile.text: Adding astrocytes felt less informative than the other steps: the result showed them around the circuit but did not add much explanation beyond the starting picture.

surprise.text: I was surprised that strengthening a synapse made the same input produce a larger local response while the travelling impulses stayed the same size.

arbitrary.text: Nothing felt purposeless, though adding oligodendrocytes followed the pictured fit of their sleeves to axons; I did not understand how myelin speeds signals from the picture alone.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: the comparisons between excitation and inhibition, and between the changed synapse and its unchanged neighbour, made me curious about what the connected cells could do next.
